title: Shantanu and Ganga
body:
PART II: THE SEEDS OF HASTINAPUR

Tracing the lineage of Hastinapur through divine births, sacred vows, ancestral curses, and the tragic seeds of sibling discord. This section analyses the transition from cosmic Dharma to the early human conflicts of the Kuru dynasty.

Shantanu and Ganga

King Shantanu was a mighty and righteous sovereign of the Chandra-Vamsha (Lunar Dynasty) who ruled the land of Hastinapur with deep devotion to Dharma. One day, while leisurely taking a stroll on the scenic banks of the river Ganga, he saw a beautiful maiden on the riverbank whose superhuman loveliness intoxicated his senses.
Drawn irresistibly by her beauty, he asked her to marry him. The maiden accepted his marriage proposal but placed a binding and strict condition: 'O king, I shall become your wife. But on certain conditions—that neither you nor anyone else should ever ask me who I am, or whence I come. You must also not stand in the way of whatever I do, good or bad, nor must you ever be wroth with me on any account whatsoever. You must not say anything displeasing to me. If you act otherwise, I shall leave you then and there. Do you agree?'
Bound by his overmastering passion, Shantanu agreed to the established conditions, and they were duly married. A few months passed, and Ganga gave birth to a beautiful baby boy. To the king's utter horror, she immediately took the infant to the river and drowned him. Shantanu, although devastated and stricken with intense grief, could not question her actions, as he was bound by his sacred promise given to her before their wedding.
One by one, Ganga gave birth to seven children, and with the same cold, unyielding silence, she drowned all seven in the river Ganga. As she was about to drown the eighth child, Shantanu could no longer control his anguish. He confronted Ganga, declaring that he had remained quiet as she drowned the previous seven children but would tolerate it no more. He pleaded for the life of the eighth son.
Ganga smiled sadly and revealed her true identity. She was the goddess Ganga, and these eight children were the Eight Vasus, cursed by Sage Vasishtha to be born mortal. The curse was a consequence of Prabhasa, the eighth Vasu, who had seized Vasishtha's sacred cow. The first seven Vasus were freed from the curse of mortal birth as soon as they were born through her act of drowning, while Prabhasa, the instigator, was destined to live a long and glorious life in the material world. True to her promise, since Shantanu had questioned her, she departed, taking the infant with her to train him for his great destiny.
She brought up the eighth child until he was a youth. This child was Devavrata. He mastered the Vedas and Vedanta from Sage Vasishtha, the arts and sciences known to Sukracharya, and the supreme art of arms under the tutelage of Sage Parasurama. Ganga eventually returned to the banks of the Yamuna, handed the resplendent prince to Shantanu, and disappeared once more.
